extracted.intended_audience: general literate public; readers of Benjamin Franklin's moral and political essays
extracted.subtask_description: Eighteenth-century moral and political essays offering practical advice, observations on civility, honesty, and liberty aimed at a general educated readership. The page collects short didactic pieces on behavior, public virtue, and free government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being critical/querulous ('leave off looking at the ugly leg')
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical, querulous, fault-finding disposition alienates others; those who constantly notice people's faults should be avoided and should themselves 'leave off looking at the ugly leg'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice and social prescription: to be respected and beloved and happy, people 'should leave off looking at the ugly leg.' Example/anti-pattern: a stranger who remarks only on a person's deformity is to be shunned. Encourages self-awareness and refraining from persistent carping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human vanity and the narrowness of temporal ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Vanity arises when creatures judge their lives only by limited, temporal measures (the 'Hypanians' who measure time by a day), mistaking short-lived achievements for true greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral illustration: the life-of-a-day insect that prides itself on long life and accomplishments exemplifies those whose ambition 'does not extend beyond the like narrow limits.' Anti-pattern: boasting of transient accomplishments that posterity will not value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as the pledge and security of lasting happiness/immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: For rational beings endowed with thought and reflection, 'virtue is the only pledge and security of a happy immortality'; temporal pleasures cannot secure lasting happiness and will cause perpetual regret if virtue is sacrificed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim and practical guidance: do not sacrifice virtue for temporal advantage, however important it seems. Example: even very long finite pleasures 'avail nothing when past' — the proper aim is virtue which secures durable happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of smuggling as dishonest and akin to theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Defrauding government of revenue by smuggling or encouraging smugglers is dishonest and morally equivalent to stealing from the public treasury; those who do so are likened to 'pickpockets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal and civic duty framing: paying taxes is a just proportion of necessary public expense; evading duties by smuggling wrongfully shifts burdens to others. Examples: buying cheaper imported luxuries, franking letters improperly; anti-pattern: treating smuggling as a harmless private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public treasure belongs to the nation — evasion harms the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: The public treasure is the nation's; when duties fall short due to smuggling and other taxes are raised to compensate, the deficit is taken from other people, often poorer citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic-economic reasoning: even small amounts (a halfpenny or farthing) taken by smugglers are effectively stolen from others. Practical implication: personal saving by evasion unjustly burdens the rest of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franking/postage evasion is an injury to revenue and dishonest
rubrics_metrics.description: When privileged persons frank letters not entitled to free postage, it is a hurt to the revenue and an injury to the nation; requesting such favors is an accompliceable crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific example: members of parliament franking private letters; social anti-pattern: respectable people freely confess intention to cheat the nation of a trifling postage without shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural relativism: 'savages' have rules of politeness too
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling people 'savages' because their manners differ is unjust; on impartial examination no nation is without rules of politeness, nor so polite as to lack rudeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical/humanistic guideline: recognise that different nations have different, coherent rules of civility. Example: Indian societies value different skills and institutions (council government, oral record-keeping) and judge British learning differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation before answering public propositions (Indian rule of politeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a rule of politeness not to answer a public proposition the same day it is made; taking time to consider shows respect for the matter's importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Six Nations at Lancaster: they defer reply until the next day, beginning by expressing thanks and then giving considered reasons. Practical implication: allow time for considered responses in public affairs; anti-pattern: immediate offhand answers treated as disrespectful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation order: silence, taking turns, and allowing recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: In council and conversation elders and speakers have ordered seating; one rises to speak, others observe silence; when a speaker sits they wait five or six minutes so he may recollect and add anything; interrupting is highly indecent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive model: Indian councils' orderly procedure contrasted with British House of Commons' interruptions and European loquacity. Practical guidance: do not interrupt, allow speakers to finish and recollect — this promotes civility and clear record-keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitality and rules for admitting strangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelling strangers should not enter a village abruptly; they announce arrival, are received by elders, placed in a strangers' house, provided victuals and bedding, and conversation begins only after refreshment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical norms for hosts and guests: the community shares resources without charge, brings tobacco and hospitality; anti-pattern: crowding and intrusive curiosity by hosts is considered rude by the visitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility can prohibit direct contradiction — caution about mistaking assent for conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Some politeness systems avoid contradiction and cultivate assent as civility, which can make it difficult to discern actual beliefs (missionaries misinterpret approbation as conversion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: politeness may mask true opinion; do not assume verbal assent equals conviction. Practical implication for persuaders: seek deeper signs of belief rather than surface civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech is a principal pillar of free government
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Freedom of speech is a principal pillar of a free government': removing it dissolves the constitution of a free society and erects tyranny on its ruins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level political principle: popular examination into magistrates' actions sustains republics and limited monarchies. Though abused, such examination is necessary; historical abuses must not be used to justify suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishing for words empowers magistrates to destroy liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting magistrates to punish speech arms them with a destructive weapon; under pretence of pruning, they may 'destroy the tree'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative caution and historical evidence: libel and punishment (Augustus, Roman examples) produced tyrannies where speech suppression led to informers, arbitrary constructions of words, and fatal outcomes for critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses of liberty are preferable to state punishment of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuses of the freedom of speech are the exercises of liberty and should be tolerated rather than assign the care of repression to magistrates, who would abuse the power to punish words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance trade-off: accept that free speech will be abused, but avoid legal mechanisms that permit judges or ministers to construe words as treason. Historical examples (Star Chamber, prosecutions under Charles I) illustrate the danger of legal repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and censorship of the stage and press corrupts arts and public morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment of licensers for stage and press leads to plays and writings that debase minds, encourage immodesty and mock religion and public spirit; censorship can pervert satire and literature into tools against virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural criticism and example: under licenser direction, comedy produced 'double entendre' and lewdness, satire aimed to debase the metropolis, and writers defended tyranny. Practical implication: licensing channels can co-opt arts to political ends and undermine public virtue.
